quotes.text: སྒྲུབ་དང་བདེན་པ་རྣམས་དང་ནི། ། སངས་རྒྱས་ལ་སོགས་དཀོན་མཆོག་གསུམ། ། མ་ཞེན་ཡོངས་སུ་མི་ངལ་དང་། ། ལམ་ནི་ཡོངས་སུ་འཛིན་པ་དང་། ། སྤྱན་ལྔ་དང་ནི་མངོན་ཤེས་ཀྱི། ། ཡོན་ཏན་དྲུག་དང་མཐོང་ལམ་དང་། ། བསྒོམ་ཞེས་བྱ་ལ་གདམས་ངག་ནི། ། བཅུ་ཡི་བདག་ཉིད་ཤེས་པར་བྱ། །
quotes.why: The Ornament's two root verses on the ten instructions: the paragraph's lemma (བསྒོམ་ཞེས་བྱ་ལ།) is their last item, and the question 'why exactly ten?' is asked of their last line.

quotes.why: The sūtra passage the paragraph cites as རབ་འབྱོར་འདུས་བྱས་ཀྱི་དབྱིངས་ཞེས་སོགས་ཀྱི་མདོ, in the Kangyur Pañcaviṃśati; it reads མ་ཡིན་པར་ཡང where the commentators quote མེད་པར. Found by direct search.

quotes.why: Haribhadra's own sentence, which the paragraph quotes whole, cited from the Tengyur: the source of 'no defined path of meditation' and of 'by the nature of dependent arising'.
Haribhadra's closing formula for the ten instructions. He says 'these alone fulfil every aim' and gives no argument for the count; the fourfold scheme that supplies one is Tibetan.

Ārya Vimuktisena, Haribhadra's source: conditioned = the path, unconditioned = abandonment, and so the path of meditation is 'nominal, not defined' — the reading that makes Haribhadra's clause sound as though there were no real path of meditation at all.
Tsongkhapa restricts Haribhadra's denial: what does not exist is a path of meditation whose way of realizing reality differs from the path of seeing's.
Tsongkhapa's answer to the same objection the paragraph answers, with the example of earlier and later water: no difference in kind, a difference in what each can do.
Tsongkhapa rejects Suvarṇadvīpa's reading of 'conditioned and unconditioned' in the sūtra example, on the authority of Vimuktisena's gloss — the one live dispute over the example itself.
The fourfold scheme — nature, object, basis, cause — that Chökyi Gyaltsen uses to fix the count at ten is Tsongkhapa's, nearly word for word.
Tsongkhapa's gloss of the last pair as causes of the final abandonment of what is to be abandoned by seeing and by meditation, with a ཁ་ཅིག alternative he records and does not adopt.
Gyaltsab Je's reformulation in terms of 'type' (རིགས་ཐ་དད), which is the wording Chökyi Gyaltsen adopts, under the same two headings (བསྒོམ་བྱ་ལམ་གྱི་རང་བཞིན་དང་རྩོད་སྤང).
Gyaltsab Je's answer to the objection, which the paragraph follows clause by clause (སྔ་མ་ལས་ … ཆེས་བསྲིངས་པའི་དབང་གིས), with his inferential-cognition example.

Gyaltsab Je in chapter four marks the end of the Mahāyāna path of seeing by the first equipoise aimed at the seeds of innate cognitive obscuration — the same object Chökyi Gyaltsen names here. Found by direct search.
Gyaltsab Je heads off the obvious objection to 'these ten alone suffice': the ten include the whole Mahāyāna path, but not all its divisions — the rest of the Ornament is not made redundant.
Panchen Sonam Drakpa (Loseling) follows Tsongkhapa's 'way of realizing reality' wording rather than Gyaltsab Je's 'type', and frames the question as one about the object realized.

Chökyi Gyaltsen's own chapter-four statement of the same structure: no difference at the level of reality, a real conventional work of diminishing the abandoned and increasing the antidote. Found by direct search.
Chökyi Gyaltsen's separate work on the twenty saṅgha opens at exactly the root verse that follows the ten instructions — where this general meaning stops. Found by direct search.
Gyaltsab Je names and rejects an earlier Tibetan view at this very point: equipoises of the ten grounds do not differ in seeing reality but do differ in seeing the dharmakāya.
Tsongkhapa's summary: both Haribhadra and Vimuktisena hold that the equipoises of all ten grounds do not differ in how they realize — the thesis the paragraph restates as 'not different in type'.
